title: Chapter 54 — The Town-Ho’s Story
paragraphs: (As told at the Golden Inn.)
The Cape of Good Hope, and all the watery region around it, is much like some notable crossroads of a great highway, where you meet more travelers than in any other part.

It was not very long after speaking the Goney that another homeward-bound whaleman, the Town-Ho,* was encountered. She was manned almost entirely by Polynesians. In the short gam that followed, she gave us strong news of Moby Dick. For some of us, the general interest in the White Whale was now wildly heightened by a circumstance of the Town-Ho's story, which seemed obscurely to involve the whale in a certain wondrous, inverted visitation of one of those so-called judgments of God that are sometimes said to overtake certain men. This circumstance, with its own particular accompaniments, forming what may be called the secret part of the tragedy about to be told, never reached the ears of Captain Ahab or his mates. For that secret part of the story was unknown even to the captain of the Town-Ho himself. It was the private property of three white seamen of that ship who were in league together, one of whom, it seems, passed it on to Tashtego under Romish injunctions of secrecy; but the following night Tashtego rambled in his sleep, and revealed so much of it that way that, when he was woken, he could not well hold back the rest. Nevertheless, so powerful an influence did this thing have on those seamen in the Pequod who came to know it fully, and by such a strange delicacy, so to call it, were they governed in this matter, that they kept the secret among themselves, so that it never traveled aft of the Pequod's mainmast. Weaving this darker thread into its proper place in the story as publicly told on the ship, I now set the whole of this strange affair down on lasting record.
*The old whale-cry raised when a whale is first sighted from the masthead; whalemen still use it today when they hunt the famous Galapagos terrapin.

For my own amusement, I will keep the style in which I once told it at Lima, to a lounging circle of Spanish friends one saint's eve, as we sat smoking on the thickly gilded, tiled terrace of the Golden Inn. Of those fine gentlemen, the young Dons Pedro and Sebastian were closest to me; hence the questions they now and then broke in with, which I answered then and there.

"Some two years before I first learned of the events I am about to recount to you, gentlemen, the Town-Ho, Sperm Whaler of Nantucket, was cruising in your Pacific here, not very many days' sail eastward from the eaves of this good Golden Inn. She was somewhere to the north of the Line (the equator). One morning, when the pumps were worked, as was the daily custom, it was noticed that she was taking more water into her hold than usual. They supposed a swordfish had stabbed her, gentlemen. But the captain had some unusual reason for believing that rare good luck awaited him in those latitudes, and was therefore very unwilling to leave them; and since the leak was not then considered at all dangerous (though, in fact, they could not find it after searching the hold as low down as was possible in rather heavy weather), the ship went on with her cruising, the sailors working at the pumps at long and easy intervals. But no good luck came. More days went by, and not only was the leak still undiscovered, but it noticeably increased. So much so that the captain, now taking some alarm, made all sail and headed for the nearest harbor among the islands, to have his hull hove out and repaired there."

"Though no short passage lay ahead of her, yet if the commonest luck held, he did not at all fear that his ship would founder on the way, because his pumps were of the best, and, taking turns at them, his thirty-six men could easily keep the ship free of water, never mind if the leak should double. In truth, since nearly the whole of this passage was attended by very favorable breezes, the Town-Ho would all but certainly have reached her port in perfect safety, without the least fatality, had it not been for the brutal overbearing of Radney, the mate, a Vineyarder from Martha's Vineyard, and the bitterly provoked vengeance of Steelkilt, a Lakeman and desperado from Buffalo."
"'Lakeman! — Buffalo! Pray, what is a Lakeman, and where is Buffalo?' said Don Sebastian, rising in his swinging grass hammock."

"On the eastern shore of our Lake Erie, Don; but — I beg your patience — perhaps you shall soon hear more of all that. Now, gentlemen, in square-sail brigs and three-masted ships, nearly as large and sturdy as any that ever sailed out of your old Callao to far Manila, this Lakeman, in the landlocked heart of our America, had nonetheless been raised on all those agrarian, freebooting impressions popularly connected with the open ocean. For taken all together, those grand freshwater seas of ours — Erie, and Ontario, and Huron, and Superior, and Michigan — have an ocean-like expanse, with many of the ocean's noblest traits, and with many of its varieties of races and climates around their rims. They contain round archipelagoes of romantic islands, just as the Polynesian waters do; for much of their length they are bordered by two great contrasting nations, as the Atlantic is; they provide long sea approaches to our many territorial colonies from the East, dotted all around their banks; here and there they are frowned upon by batteries, and by the goat-like, craggy guns of lofty Mackinaw; they have heard the swift thunder of naval victories; at intervals they yield their beaches to wild barbarians, whose red-painted faces flash out from their fur-hide wigwams; for leagues and leagues they are flanked by ancient, untrodden forests, where the gaunt pines stand like serried lines of kings in Gothic family trees, those same woods sheltering wild African beasts of prey, and silky-coated creatures whose exported furs make robes for Tartar Emperors; they mirror the paved capitals of Buffalo and Cleveland, as well as Winnebago villages; they float alike the full-rigged merchant ship, the armed cruiser of the State, the steamer, and the beech canoe; they are swept by north winds and dismasting blasts as terrible as any that lash the salt sea; they know what shipwrecks are, for out of sight of land, however inland, they have drowned many a ship at midnight with all its shrieking crew. So, gentlemen, though an inlander, Steelkilt was born to the wild ocean and raised on the wild ocean — as bold a mariner as any. And as for Radney: though as an infant he may have lain down on the lonely Nantucket beach to nurse at his mother the sea; though in later life he had long followed our austere Atlantic and your contemplative Pacific — he was still quite as vengeful and quarrelsome as the backwoods seaman fresh from the latitudes of buckhorn-handled Bowie knives. Yet this Nantucketer was a man with some good-hearted traits; and this Lakeman was a mariner who, though a sort of devil indeed, could still be handled by unbending firmness, tempered only by that common decency of human recognition which is the right of the lowliest slave; treated that way, this Steelkilt had long been kept harmless and docile. At any rate, he had proved so up to then; but Radney was doomed and driven mad, and Steelkilt — but, gentlemen, you shall hear."

"It was not more than a day or two at most after she had pointed her bow toward her island harbor that the Town-Ho's leak seemed to be increasing again, though only enough to require an hour or more at the pumps every day. You must know that in a settled and civilized ocean like our Atlantic, for example, some captains think little of pumping their whole way across it — though on a still, sleepy night, should the officer of the deck happen to forget his duty in that respect, the likelihood is that he and his shipmates would never remember it again, because all hands would be gently settling to the bottom. Nor in the lonely and savage seas far to the west of you, gentlemen, is it altogether unusual for ships to keep clanging at their pump-handles in full chorus even over a voyage of considerable length; that is, if it runs along a fairly accessible coast, or if some other reasonable refuge is open to them. It is only when a leaky vessel is in some very out-of-the-way part of those waters, some truly landless latitude, that her captain begins to feel a little anxious."

"Much this way it had been with the Town-Ho. So when her leak was found gaining once more, there was in truth some small concern shown by several of her company, especially by Radney the mate. He ordered the upper sails to be well hoisted, sheeted home anew, and every way spread to the breeze. Now this Radney, I suppose, was as little of a coward, and as little inclined to any sort of nervous fear for his own person, as any fearless, unthinking creature on land or on sea that you can conveniently imagine, gentlemen. So when he showed this anxiety about the safety of the ship, some of the seamen declared that it was only because he was a part owner in her. And so, when they were working at the pumps that evening, there was no small amount of sly joking going on among them on this point, as they stood with their feet continually washed over by the rippling clear water — clear as any mountain spring, gentlemen — that bubbled from the pumps, ran across the deck, and poured itself out in steady spouts at the lee scupper-holes."

"Now, as you well know, it quite often happens in this conventional world of ours — watery or otherwise — that when a man put in command over his fellows finds that one of them is markedly his superior in general pride of manhood, he at once takes an unconquerable dislike and bitterness toward that man; and given the chance, he will tear down that subordinate's tower and grind it into a little heap of dust. Whatever you make of this notion of mine, gentlemen, Steelkilt at any rate was a tall and noble animal, with a head like a Roman's and a flowing golden beard like the tasseled trappings of your last viceroy's snorting charger; and he had a brain, and a heart, and a soul in him, gentlemen, that would have made Steelkilt Charlemagne, had he been born the son of Charlemagne's father. But Radney, the mate, was as ugly as a mule — and just as hardy, just as stubborn, just as malicious. He had no love for Steelkilt, and Steelkilt knew it."
"Spotting the mate drawing near as he was toiling at the pump with the rest, the Lakeman pretended not to notice him, but, not in the least intimidated, went on with his cheerful banter."

"'Aye, aye, my merry lads, it's a lively leak this! Hold a cup, one of you, and let's have a taste. By the Lord, it's worth bottling! I tell you what, men, old Rad's investment must go for it! He'd best cut away his part of the hull and tow it home. The fact is, boys, that swordfish only started the job. He's come back again with a gang of ship-carpenters, sawfish, and filefish, and what not; and the whole posse of them are now hard at work cutting and slashing at the bottom — making improvements, I suppose. If old Rad were here now, I'd tell him to jump overboard and scatter them. They're playing the devil with his estate, I can tell him. But he's a simple old soul, Rad, and a beauty too. Boys, they say the rest of his property is invested in looking-glasses. I wonder if he'd give a poor devil like me the model of his nose.'"
"'Damn your eyes! What's that pump stopping for?' roared Radney, pretending not to have heard the sailors' talk. 'Thunder away at it!'"

"'Aye, aye, sir,' said Steelkilt, merry as a cricket. 'Lively, boys, lively, now!' And with that the pump clanged like fifty fire-engines. The men tossed their hats off to it, and before long that peculiar gasping of the lungs was heard that marks the fullest strain of life's utmost energies."

"Leaving the pump at last with the rest of his gang, the Lakeman went forward all panting and sat himself down on the windlass, his face fiery red, his eyes bloodshot, wiping the heavy sweat from his brow. Now what deceiving fiend it was, gentlemen, that possessed Radney to meddle with such a man in that physically inflamed state, I don't know; but so it happened. Striding intolerably along the deck, the mate ordered him to get a broom and sweep down the planks, and also a shovel, and clear away some offensive matter left from letting a pig run loose."

"Now, gentlemen, sweeping a ship's deck at sea is a piece of housework that, in all weather but raging gales, is regularly attended to every evening; it has been known to be done on ships that were actually sinking at the time. Such, gentlemen, is the inflexibility of sea customs and the instinctive love of neatness in seamen, some of whom would not willingly drown without first washing their faces. But in all vessels this broom business is, by long-established right, the province of the boys, if there are boys aboard. Besides, it was the stronger men in the Town-Ho who had been divided into gangs, taking turns at the pumps; and being the most athletic seaman of them all, Steelkilt had been regularly appointed captain of one of the gangs. So he should have been excused from any trivial business not connected with truly nautical duties, as his comrades were. I mention all these details so that you may understand exactly how this affair stood between the two men."

"But there was more than this: the order about the shovel was almost as plainly meant to sting and insult Steelkilt as if Radney had spat in his face. Any man who has gone to sea as a sailor in a whale-ship will understand this; and all this, and doubtless much more, the Lakeman fully grasped when the mate gave his command. But as he sat still for a moment, and as he steadily looked into the mate's malignant eye and saw the stacks of powder-casks heaped up inside him and the slow-match silently burning along toward them — as he instinctively saw all this, that strange forbearance, that unwillingness to stir up the deeper passions of any already angry being — a reluctance felt most, when it is felt at all, by truly brave men even when they have been wronged — this nameless phantom feeling, gentlemen, stole over Steelkilt."

"Therefore, in his ordinary tone, only a little broken by the physical exhaustion he was in for the moment, he answered that sweeping the deck was not his business, and he would not do it. And then, without mentioning the shovel at all, he pointed to three lads as the usual sweepers, who, not being assigned to the pumps, had done little or nothing all day. To this Radney replied with an oath, repeating his command without condition in a most domineering and outrageous manner, and meanwhile advancing on the still-seated Lakeman with a raised cooper's club hammer, which he had snatched from a cask nearby."

"Heated and irritated as he was by his convulsive labor at the pumps, for all his initial nameless impulse to hold back, the sweating Steelkilt could barely stand this behavior from the mate. But somehow still smothering the fire within him, without speaking he remained stubbornly rooted to his seat, until at last the enraged Radney shook the hammer within a few inches of his face, furiously commanding him to obey."

"Steelkilt rose, and slowly retreating around the windlass, steadily followed by the mate with his threatening hammer, deliberately repeated his intention not to obey. Seeing, however, that his forbearance had not the slightest effect, he warned off the foolish, infatuated man with an awful and unspeakable signal of his twisted hand; but it was no use. And in this way the two went slowly once around the windlass; then, resolved at last to retreat no further, and reflecting that he had now put up with as much as suited his temper, the Lakeman stopped on the hatches and spoke to the officer as follows:"

"'Mr. Radney, I will not obey you. Take that hammer away, or look out for yourself.' But the predestined mate, coming still closer to where the Lakeman stood fixed, now shook the heavy hammer within an inch of his teeth, meanwhile repeating a string of unbearable curses. Not retreating the thousandth part of an inch, stabbing him in the eye with the unflinching dagger of his glance, Steelkilt, clenching his right hand behind him and stealthily drawing it back, told his persecutor that if the hammer so much as grazed his cheek, he (Steelkilt) would murder him. But, gentlemen, the fool had been branded for the slaughter by the gods. Immediately the hammer touched the cheek; the next instant the mate's lower jaw was smashed in against his head; he fell on the hatch spouting blood like a whale."
"Before the shout could travel aft, Steelkilt was already shaking one of the backstays that ran far up to where two of his comrades stood their watch at the mastheads. Both of them were Canallers."
"'Canallers!' cried Don Pedro. 'We have seen many whale-ships in our harbors, but never heard of your Canallers. Pardon — who and what are they?'"
"'Canallers, Don, are the boatmen of our great Erie Canal. You must have heard of it.'"
"'No, Senor. Hereabouts in this dull, warm, most lazy, and hereditary land, we know but little of your vigorous North.'"
"'Is that so? Well then, Don, refill my cup. Your chicha is very fine. And before going further I will tell you what our Canallers are, for such information may shed light on my story.'"

"For three hundred and sixty miles, gentlemen, through the entire breadth of the state of New York; through numerous populous cities and most thriving villages; through long, dismal, uninhabited swamps, and rich cultivated fields unrivaled for fertility; by billiard-room and bar-room; through the holy of holies of great forests; on Roman arches over Indian rivers; through sun and shade; by happy hearts or broken; through all the wide, contrasting scenery of those noble Mohawk counties; and especially by rows of snow-white chapels, whose spires stand almost like milestones — there flows one continuous stream of life as corrupt as Venice's and often lawless. There's your true Ashantee, gentlemen; there your pagans howl; where you always find them, next door to you, under the long-cast shadow and the snug, patronizing shelter of churches. For by some curious fatality, just as it is often noted that your big-city robbers always camp around the halls of justice, so sinners, gentlemen, most abound in the holiest neighborhoods."
"'Is that a friar passing?' said Don Pedro, looking down into the crowded plaza with humorous concern."
"'Well for our northern friend that Dame Isabella's Inquisition is waning in Lima,' laughed Don Sebastian. 'Proceed, Senor.'"

"'A moment! Pardon!' cried another of the company. 'In the name of all us Limeese, I only wish to say to you, sir sailor, that we have by no means overlooked your delicacy in not substituting present-day Lima for distant Venice in your comparison of corruption. Oh! Do not bow and look surprised; you know the proverb all along this coast: "Corrupt as Lima." It only bears out your saying, too: churches more plentiful than billiard-tables, and forever open — and "Corrupt as Lima." So too with Venice; I have been there — the holy city of the blessed evangelist, St. Mark! — St. Dominic, purge it! Your cup! Thanks — here I refill; now, you pour out again.'"

"Freely portrayed in his own calling, gentlemen, the Canaller would make a fine dramatic hero, so abundantly and picturesquely wicked is he. Like Mark Antony, for days and days along his green-turfed, flowery Nile, he lazily floats, openly toying with his red-cheeked Cleopatra, ripening his apricot thigh on the sunny deck. But ashore, all this softness is dashed away. The brigand-like getup the Canaller so proudly sports, and his slouched and gaily ribboned hat, proclaim his grand features. A terror to the smiling innocence of the villages he floats through, his swarthy face and bold swagger are shunned in the cities too. Once, when I was a vagabond on his own canal, I received good turns from one of these Canallers; I thank him heartily, and would not wish to be ungrateful; but it is often one of the chief redeeming qualities of your man of violence that at times he has as stiff an arm to back a poor stranger in a tight spot as to rob a wealthy one. In sum, gentlemen, how wild this canal life is, is emphatically shown by this: that our wild whale-fishery contains so many of its most finished graduates, and that hardly any breed of men, except Sydney men, are so much distrusted by our whaling captains. Nor does it at all lessen the curiousness of this matter that, for many thousands of our country boys and young men born along its route, the probationary life of the Grand Canal furnishes the only transition between quietly reaping in a Christian cornfield and recklessly plowing the waters of the most barbaric seas."

"'I see! I see!' exclaimed Don Pedro eagerly, spilling his chicha on his silver ruffles. 'No need to travel! The world's one Lima. I had thought, now, that in your temperate North the generations were cold and holy as the hills. — But the story.'"

"I stopped, gentlemen, at the point where the Lakeman shook the backstay. He had barely done it when the three junior mates and the four harpooners surrounded him and all crowded him down to the deck. But the two Canallers slid down the ropes like baleful comets, rushed into the uproar, and tried to drag their man out of it toward the forecastle. Some of the other sailors joined them in the attempt, and a twisting scramble broke out; meanwhile the valiant captain, keeping well out of harm's way, danced up and down with a whale-pike, calling on his officers to rough up that atrocious scoundrel and drive him aft to the quarter-deck. Every so often he ran up close to the whirling edge of the confusion and poked into the middle of it with his pike, trying to prick out the man he resented. But Steelkilt and his desperadoes were too much for all of them. They managed to reach the forecastle deck, and there, quickly swinging three or four big casks around into a line with the windlass, these sea-Parisians dug in behind the barricade."
"'Come out of that, you pirates!' roared the captain, now threatening them with a pistol in each hand, just brought to him by the steward. 'Come out of that, you cutthroats!'"

"Steelkilt leaped on the barricade, and striding up and down there, defied the worst the pistols could do. But he gave the captain to understand clearly that his — Steelkilt's — death would be the signal for a murderous mutiny from all hands. Fearing in his heart that this might prove all too true, the captain backed off a little, but still commanded the rebels to return immediately to their duty."
"'Will you promise not to touch us if we do?' demanded their ringleader."
"'Turn to! Turn to! — I make no promise — to your duty! Do you want to sink the ship by knocking off at a time like this? Turn to!' And he once more raised a pistol."

"'Sink the ship?' cried Steelkilt. 'Aye, let her sink. Not a man of us turns to unless you swear not to raise so much as a rope-yarn against us. What say you, men?' turning to his comrades. A fierce cheer was their response."

"The Lakeman now paced up and down behind the barricade, never taking his eye off the Captain, and jerking out sentences like these: 'It's not our fault; we didn't want this; I told him to take his hammer away; it was a job for a boy; he ought to have known me by now; I told him not to prod the buffalo; I think I've broken a finger here on his cursed jaw; aren't those mincing knives down in the forecastle, men? Keep an eye on those handspikes, my hearties. Captain, by God, watch yourself; say the word; don't be a fool; forget the whole thing; we're ready to turn to; treat us decently and we're your men; but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to! I make no promises. Turn to, I say!'"

"'Look here, now,' cried the Lakeman, flinging out his arm toward him, 'there are a few of us here — and I am one of them — who have shipped for the cruise, do you see? Now as you well know, sir, we can claim our discharge as soon as the anchor is down. So we don't want a fight. It's not in our interest. We want to be peaceable. We are ready to work, but we won't be flogged.'"
"'Turn to!' roared the Captain."

"Steelkilt glanced around him a moment, and then said: 'I tell you what it is now, Captain — rather than kill you, and be hanged for such a shabby rascal, we won't lift a hand against you unless you attack us. But until you give us the word about not flogging us, we don't do a hand's turn.'"
"'Down into the forecastle, then. Down with you! I'll keep you there till you're sick of it. Down you go.'"

"'Shall we?' cried the ringleader to his men. Most of them were against it. But at length, in obedience to Steelkilt, they preceded him down into their dark den, disappearing with growls, like bears into a cave."

"As the Lakeman's bare head was just level with the planks, the Captain and his posse leaped the barricade, and, rapidly drawing the slide of the scuttle over, all planted their hands on it and loudly called for the steward to bring the heavy brass padlock belonging to the companionway. Then, opening the slide a little, the Captain whispered something down the crack, closed it, and turned the key on them — ten in number — leaving on deck some twenty or more, who so far had remained neutral."

"All night a wide-awake watch was kept by all the officers, fore and aft, especially about the forecastle scuttle and the fore hatchway, where it was feared the rebels might come out after breaking through the bulkhead below. But the hours of darkness passed in peace, the men who still remained at their duty toiling hard at the pumps, whose clinking and clanking, at intervals through the dreary night, echoed dismally through the ship."

"At sunrise the Captain went forward, and, knocking on the deck, summoned the prisoners to work; but with a yell they refused. Water was then lowered down to them, and a couple of handfuls of biscuit were tossed after it; then, locking them in again and pocketing the key, the Captain returned to the quarter-deck. Twice a day for three days this was repeated; but on the fourth morning, as the usual summons was delivered, a confused wrangling and then a scuffling was heard, and suddenly four men burst up from the forecastle, saying they were ready to turn to. The stifling, foul air and a starvation diet, together perhaps with some fear of final punishment, had forced them to surrender unconditionally. Emboldened by this, the Captain repeated his demand to the rest, but Steelkilt shouted up to him a terrific hint to stop his babbling and take himself off where he belonged. On the fifth morning three others of the mutineers bolted up into the air, breaking free from the desperate arms below that tried to hold them back. Only three were left."
"'Better turn to, now?' said the Captain with a heartless jeer."
"'Shut us up again, will you!' cried Steelkilt."
"'Oh certainly,' said the Captain, and the key clicked."

"It was at this point, gentlemen, that — enraged by the defection of seven of his former comrades, stung by the mocking voice that had last hailed him, and maddened by his long entombment in a place as black as the bowels of despair — it was then that Steelkilt proposed to the two Canallers, who so far had seemed to be of one mind with him, that they burst out of their hole at the next summons from the garrison and, armed with their keen mincing knives (long, crescent-shaped, heavy implements with a handle at each end), run amok from the bowsprit to the taffrail, and, if any devilish desperation could make it possible, seize the ship. For himself, he said, he would do this whether they joined him or not. That was the last night he would spend in that den. But the scheme met no opposition from the other two; they swore they were ready for that, or for any other mad thing — for anything, in short, but surrender. And what was more, each of them insisted on being the first man on deck when the time came to make the rush. But to this their leader objected just as fiercely, reserving that place for himself, especially as his two comrades would not give way to each other on the matter, and both of them could not be first, for the ladder would admit only one man at a time. And here, gentlemen, the foul play of these villains must come out."

"On hearing their leader's frantic plan, each of them, in his own separate soul, had suddenly hit, it would seem, on the same piece of treachery: namely, to be foremost in breaking out, so as to be the first of the three, though the last of the ten, to surrender, and thereby secure whatever small chance of pardon such conduct might earn. But when Steelkilt made known his determination still to lead them to the last, they somehow, by some subtle chemistry of villainy, mixed their until then secret treacheries together; and when their leader fell into a doze, they opened their souls to each other in three sentences, and bound the sleeper with cords, and gagged him with cords, and shrieked out for the Captain at midnight."

"Thinking murder was at hand, and smelling in the dark for the blood, he and all his armed mates and harpooners rushed for the forecastle. In a few minutes the scuttle was opened, and, bound hand and foot, the still-struggling ringleader was shoved up into the air by his treacherous allies, who at once claimed the honor of securing a man who had been fully ripe for murder. But all of them were collared and dragged along the deck like dead cattle; and, side by side, they were lashed up in the mizzen rigging like three quarters of meat, and there they hung till morning. 'Damn you,' cried the Captain, pacing back and forth in front of them, 'the vultures wouldn't touch you, you villains!'"

"At sunrise he summoned all hands, and, separating those who had rebelled from those who had taken no part in the mutiny, he told the former that he had a good mind to flog them all round — thought, on the whole, he would do so — he ought to — justice demanded it; but for the present, considering their timely surrender, he would let them go with a reprimand, which he duly delivered in the plain vernacular."

"'But as for you, you carrion rogues,' turning to the three men in the rigging, 'for you, I mean to mince you up for the try-pots.' And, seizing a rope, he applied it with all his might to the backs of the two traitors, until they yelled no more, but hung their heads lifelessly sideways, as the two crucified thieves are drawn."

"'My wrist is sprained with you!' he cried at last. 'But there is still rope enough left for you, my fine bantam, who wouldn't give up. Take that gag from his mouth, and let us hear what he can say for himself.'"

"For a moment the exhausted mutineer made a trembling motion of his cramped jaws, and then painfully twisting his head around, said in a sort of hiss, 'What I say is this — and mind it well — if you flog me, I murder you!'"
"'You say so? Then see how you frighten me' — and the Captain drew back with the rope to strike."
"'Best not,' hissed the Lakeman."
"'But I must' — and the rope was once more drawn back for the stroke."

"Steelkilt here hissed out something inaudible to all but the Captain, who, to the amazement of all hands, started back, paced the deck rapidly two or three times, and then suddenly throwing down his rope, said, 'I won't do it — let him go — cut him down, do you hear?'"

"But as the junior mates were hurrying to carry out the order, a pale man with a bandaged head stopped them — Radney, the chief mate. Ever since the blow, he had lain in his berth; but that morning, hearing the commotion on deck, he had crept out, and so far had watched the whole scene. His mouth was in such a state that he could hardly speak; but mumbling something about how he, for one, was willing and able to do what the captain dared not attempt, he snatched the rope and advanced on his bound enemy."
"'You are a coward!' hissed the Lakeman."

"'So I am — but take that.' The mate was just about to strike when another hiss held back his raised arm. He paused; and then, pausing no longer, he carried out what he had said, in spite of Steelkilt's threat, whatever it might have been. The three men were then cut down and all hands were sent back to work, and, sullenly manned by the moody seamen, the iron pumps clanged just as before."

"Just after dark that day, when one watch had gone below, a commotion was heard in the forecastle; and the two trembling traitors came running up and besieged the cabin door, saying they dared not stay among the crew. Pleas, cuffs, and kicks could not drive them back, so at their own request they were put down in the ship's run, the narrow afterpart of her hold, for their salvation. Still, no sign of mutiny reappeared among the rest. On the contrary, it seemed that, mainly at Steelkilt's urging, they had resolved to keep the strictest peace, obey all orders to the last, and, when the ship reached port, desert her in a body. But in order to ensure the quickest end to the voyage, they all agreed to one thing more — namely, not to sing out for whales if any should be discovered. For in spite of her leak, and in spite of all her other dangers, the Town-Ho still kept men at her mastheads, and her captain was just as willing to lower for a whale at that moment as on the day his ship first reached the cruising ground; and Radney the mate was quite as ready to trade his berth for a boat, and with his bandaged mouth try to gag the whale's living jaw in death."

"But though the Lakeman had persuaded the seamen to adopt this sort of passiveness in their conduct, he kept his own counsel (at least till all was over) about his own proper and private revenge on the man who had stung him in the very ventricles of his heart. He was in Radney the chief mate's watch; and, as if the infatuated man were trying to run more than halfway to meet his doom, after the scene at the rigging he insisted, against the captain's express advice, on resuming the command of his watch at night. On this, and on one or two other circumstances, Steelkilt systematically built the plan of his revenge."

"During the night, Radney had an unseamanlike way of sitting on the bulwarks of the quarter-deck and leaning his arm on the gunwale of the boat that was hoisted up there, a little above the ship's side. In this position, it was well known, he sometimes dozed. There was a considerable gap between the boat and the ship, and down through it lay the sea. Steelkilt calculated his time, and found that his next trick (his turn of duty) at the helm would come round at two o'clock in the morning of the third day from the one on which he had been betrayed. At his leisure, he spent the interval braiding something very carefully during his watches below."
"'What are you making there?' said a shipmate."
"'What do you think? What does it look like?'"
"'Like a lanyard for your bag. But it's an odd one, seems to me.'"
"'Yes, rather odd,' said the Lakeman, holding it at arm's length before him. 'But I think it will do. Shipmate, I haven't enough twine — have you any?'"
"But there was none in the forecastle."
"'Then I must get some from old Rad.' And he rose to go aft."
"'You don't mean to go begging to him, of all people!' said a sailor."

"'Why not? Do you think he won't do me a turn, when it's to help himself in the end, shipmate?' And going to the mate, he looked at him quietly and asked him for some twine to mend his hammock. It was given him — neither twine nor lanyard was ever seen again; but the next night an iron ball, closely netted, partly rolled out of the pocket of the Lakeman's monkey jacket as he was tucking the coat into his hammock for a pillow. Twenty-four hours later would come his trick at the silent helm — close beside the man who was apt to doze over the grave always dug ready to the seaman's hand — and that would be the fatal hour; and in the foreordaining soul of Steelkilt, the mate already lay stark and stretched out as a corpse, with his forehead crushed in."

"But, gentlemen, a fool saved the would-be murderer from the bloody deed he had planned. And yet he got his revenge in full without being the one to take it. For through some mysterious fatality, it seemed as if Heaven itself stepped in and took the damning thing he would have done out of his hands and into its own."

"It was just between daybreak and sunrise on the morning of the second day, while they were washing down the decks, that a dim-witted man from Tenerife, drawing water in the main-chains, suddenly shouted, 'There she rolls! There she rolls!' Jesu, what a whale! It was Moby Dick."
"'Moby Dick!' cried Don Sebastian. 'St. Dominic! Sir sailor, but do whales have christenings? Whom do you call Moby Dick?'"
"'A very white, and famous, and most deadly immortal monster, Don — but that would be too long a story.'"
"'How? How?' cried all the young Spaniards, crowding around."
"'No, Dons, Dons — no, no! I cannot tell that now. Let me get more into the air, Sirs.'"
"'The chicha! The chicha!' cried Don Pedro. 'Our vigorous friend looks faint — fill up his empty glass!'"

"No need, gentlemen; one moment, and I'll go on. — Now, gentlemen, suddenly seeing the snowy whale within fifty yards of the ship — forgetting the pact among the crew — in the excitement of the moment the Tenerife man had instinctively and involuntarily raised his voice for the monster, though for some little time past it had been plainly visible from the three sullen mastheads. Everything was now a frenzy. 'The White Whale — the White Whale!' was the cry from captain, mates, and harpooners, who, undeterred by fearful rumors, were all eager to capture so famous and precious a fish; while the sullen crew eyed sideways, and with curses, the appalling beauty of the vast milky mass that, lit up by the level, spangling rays of the sun, shifted and glistened like a living opal in the blue morning sea. Gentlemen, a strange fatality runs through the whole course of these events, as if truly mapped out before the world itself was charted. The mutineer was the mate's bowsman, and when they were fast to a whale, it was his duty to sit next to him, while Radney stood up with his lance in the bow, and to haul in or slacken the line at the word of command. Moreover, when the four boats were lowered, the mate's got the start; and no one howled more fiercely with delight than Steelkilt as he strained at his oar. After a hard pull, their harpooner got fast, and, spear in hand, Radney sprang to the bow. He was always a furious man in a boat, it seems. And now his bandaged cry was to beach him on the whale's topmost back. Only too willing, his bowsman hauled him up and up, through a blinding foam that blended two whitenesses together, until suddenly the boat struck as if against a sunken ledge, and, tipping over, spilled out the standing mate. At that instant, as he fell on the whale's slippery back, the boat righted and was dashed aside by the swell, while Radney was tossed over into the sea on the other flank of the whale. He struck out through the spray, and for an instant was dimly seen through that veil, wildly trying to get himself out of the eye of Moby Dick. But the whale rushed around in a sudden maelstrom, seized the swimmer between his jaws, and, rearing high up with him, plunged headlong again and went down."

"Meanwhile, at the first bump of the boat's bottom, the Lakeman had slackened the line so as to drop astern out of the whirlpool; calmly looking on, he thought his own thoughts. But a sudden, terrific, downward jerk of the boat quickly brought his knife to the line. He cut it, and the whale was free. But at some distance Moby Dick rose again, with some tatters of Radney's red woolen shirt caught in the teeth that had destroyed him. All four boats gave chase again; but the whale eluded them, and finally disappeared altogether."

"In good time, the Town-Ho reached her port — a savage, solitary place where no civilized creature lived. There, led by the Lakeman, all but five or six of the foremast hands deliberately deserted among the palms, eventually, as it turned out, seizing a large double war-canoe of the savages and setting sail for some other harbor."

"With the ship's company reduced to just a handful, the captain called on the Islanders to help him in the laborious business of heaving down the ship to stop the leak. But this small band of whites was forced to keep such unresting watch over their dangerous allies, both by night and by day, and the hard work they went through was so extreme, that when the vessel was ready for sea again they were so weakened that the captain dared not set out with them in so heavy a vessel. After consulting with his officers, he anchored the ship as far offshore as possible, loaded and ran out his two cannon from the bows, stacked his muskets on the poop, and, warning the Islanders not to approach the ship at their peril, took one man with him, set the sail of his best whaleboat, and steered straight before the wind for Tahiti, five hundred miles away, to get reinforcements for his crew."

"On the fourth day of sailing, they spotted a large canoe that seemed to have put in at a low coral island. The captain steered away from it, but the savage craft came bearing down on him, and soon Steelkilt's voice hailed him, ordering him to heave to or be run under water. He leveled a pistol. Standing with one foot on each prow of the lashed-together war-canoes, the Lakeman laughed him to scorn, and told him that if the pistol so much as clicked in its lock, he would bury him in bubbles and foam."
"'What do you want of me?' cried the captain."
"'Where are you bound? And for what are you bound?' demanded Steelkilt. 'No lies.'"
"'I am bound to Tahiti for more men.'"
"'Very good. Let me board you a moment — I come in peace.' With that he leaped from the canoe, swam to the boat, and climbing the gunwale, stood face to face with the captain."

"'Cross your arms, sir. Throw back your head. Now, repeat after me. As soon as Steelkilt leaves me, I swear to beach this boat on that island and remain there six days. If I do not, may lightning strike me!'"
"'A pretty scholar,' laughed the Lakeman. 'Adios, Senor!' And leaping into the sea, he swam back to his comrades."

"Watching the boat until it was fairly beached and drawn up to the roots of the coconut trees, Steelkilt set sail again, and in due time arrived at Tahiti, his own destination. There luck befriended him. Two ships were about to sail for France and were providentially in need of precisely the number of men the sailor led. They embarked, and so forever got the start of their former captain, had he been at all inclined to bring legal retribution on them."

"About ten days after the French ships sailed, the whale-boat arrived, and the captain had to sign on some of the more civilized Tahitians, who had some experience of the sea. He chartered a small native schooner, went back with them to his ship, found everything in order there, and took up his cruising again."

"Where Steelkilt now is, gentlemen, no one knows; but on the island of Nantucket, the widow of Radney still turns to the sea that refuses to give up its dead, and still in dreams sees the awful white whale that destroyed him. * * * *"
"'Are you through?' said Don Sebastian quietly."
"'I am, Don.'"

"'Then I beg you, tell me: to the best of your own belief, is this story of yours really true in substance? It is so extraordinarily wonderful! Did you have it from a source beyond question? Forgive me if I seem to press.'"
"'Also bear with all of us, sir sailor, for we all join in Don Sebastian's request,' cried the company, with great interest."
"'Is there a copy of the Holy Evangelists, the Gospels, in the Golden Inn, gentlemen?'"
"'No,' said Don Sebastian, 'but I know a worthy priest nearby who will quickly get one for me. I go for it — but are you sure about this? This may grow too serious.'"
"'Will you be so good as to bring the priest also, Don?'"

"'Though there are no Auto-da-Fés in Lima now,' said one of the company to another, 'I fear our sailor friend runs the risk of the archbishop's attention. Let us move farther out of the moonlight. I see no need for this.'"
"'Excuse me for running after you, Don Sebastian; but may I also ask that you will be particular in getting the largest-sized Evangelists you can.'"
"'This is the priest; he brings you the Evangelists,' said Don Sebastian gravely, returning with a tall and solemn figure."
"'Let me take off my hat. Now, venerable priest, come farther into the light, and hold the Holy Book up in front of me so that I can touch it.'"

"'So help me Heaven, and on my honor the story I have told you, gentlemen, is in substance and its great items, true. I know it to be true. It happened on this earth. I walked that ship. I knew the crew. I have seen and talked with Steelkilt since the death of Radney.'"
